info.name: Cobre Notifications — full demo
info.description:
The entire demo, driven from Postman. No terminal.

The folders are numbered in the order they are meant to be run, and each one maps to a section of `docs/DEMO_RUNBOOK.md`.

**Two kinds of request live here.**

The *product* APIs — self-service (3002) and subscriptions (3001) — are what a real client calls. Every one of them requires a bearer token, and the client identity comes from the token's `sub` claim. No endpoint accepts a `client_id` parameter: that is the access-control model.

The *simulation* endpoints on demo-tools (3004) stand in for two things that are not part of the product: the platform microservices that emit business events, and a client's webhook endpoint. They need no auth and never run in a real deployment.

**Tokens.** `0 · Setup / Get a token` fetches one explicitly, and a collection-level pre-request script also fetches one automatically whenever `client_id` changes — so switching the `client_id` variable to `CLIENT002` and re-running any request demonstrates tenant isolation immediately.

variable.description: On presentation day, replace with the public HTTPS URL the panel provides.

exec: // Fetch a token on demand, and re-fetch whenever client_id changes,
// so switching client demonstrates tenant isolation with no extra steps.
// Skipped for the token request itself and for demo-tools, which
// simulates infrastructure and takes no auth.
body: { mode: 'raw', raw: JSON.stringify({ client_id: clientId }) }

item.name: 0 · Setup
item.description: Run these three in order. Roughly 30 seconds, and the platform is holding the case statement's own dataset, delivered for real.

request.description:
A demo affordance, mounted only when `ENABLE_DEMO_TOKENS=true`. A real deployment obtains tokens from the platform's identity provider — the middleware is where that changes, and nothing else moves.

The token is HS256 with the algorithm pinned and the issuer and audience validated. Its `sub` claim is the client identity, and it is the only source of it anywhere in the platform.

Both APIs share the issuer and audience, so one token works against self-service and subscriptions alike.

The response is stored in the `token` variable, but the collection also fetches one automatically — you do not have to run this first. It is here so the token flow is visible rather than hidden in a script.

exec: // The claim the whole access-control model rests on.

request.description:
Registers one subscription per (client, event type) pair in the fixture — ten in total across three clients.

It goes through the **public** subscription API, so the SSRF guard runs and a signing secret is issued for each one, exactly as it would for a real client. The secrets are then handed to the demo webhook receiver, which is how a real client stores them: keyed by client and event type, since each subscription gets its own.

**On presentation day**, set the `webhook_url` variable to the public HTTPS URL the panel provides and run this.

exec: console.log('signing secrets handed to the receiver:', body.secretsHandedToReceiver);

request.description:
Publishes all ten events from `fixtures/notification_events.json` onto the delivery topic, standing in for the platform's own producers.

This is the case statement's Task 2, executed: *obtain the list of notifications from a repository (the attached file) and deliver them via a webhook to a public https URL*.

Nothing here knows a webhook exists. It publishes an event and stops.

Watch the operations dashboard at {{monitor}} while this runs.

The deliveries as they arrived at the client's side, with the traceability headers and — crucially — the result of verifying the HMAC signature.

`signature: "valid"` means the receiver recomputed HMAC-SHA256 over `<timestamp>.<raw body>` with that subscription's own secret and got the same value, in constant time, within a five-minute window.

item.name: 2 · Failure, retry and exhaustion
item.description:
Run these in order to watch one event travel the whole lifecycle. Roughly a minute.

The demo webhook fails on request, not at random — the previous mock returned 500 half the time, which made this impossible to demonstrate reliably.

request.description:
The next 50 deliveries return 500 — enough to spend a whole retry budget without the endpoint recovering mid-way.

Other modes:
- `{"status": 503}` — every delivery fails
- `{"delayMs": 6000}` — every delivery hangs, to demonstrate the timeout
- `{"reset": true}` — back to succeeding

Stands in for a platform microservice emitting a business event.

Omit `event_id` and a fresh one is generated. Send the **same** `event_id` twice to demonstrate idempotency: the second publish creates nothing new, because `event_id` is a unique constraint and the dispatcher re-reads the existing row.

Now watch the dashboard: attempt 1 `SYSTEM` fails, then `RETRY_SERVICE` attempts appear with growing gaps, then the event reaches `FAILED`. About 45 seconds with the demo retry settings.

item.name: Find it once the budget is spent

request.description:
Wait ~45 seconds after publishing, then run this. The event appears as `FAILED` — the state the retry service writes when the budget runs out, and the only state the replay endpoint accepts.

This is what was unreachable in the previous version: a failed delivery went back to `PENDING`, so nothing ever declared an event definitively failed, and the replay endpoint guarded on the wrong states.

exec: console.log('not FAILED yet — give the retry budget a few more seconds');

request.description: Run this before replaying, so the replay has something to succeed against.

Then open `1 · Notification events / Detail` and look at the attempts:

| attempt | origin | status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | SYSTEM | FAILED |
| 2–5 | RETRY_SERVICE | FAILED |
| 6 | SELF_SERVICE | SUCCESS |

Six attempts, three origins, one pipeline. They differ in one field, which exists so this table can tell them apart — there is no second implementation of delivery that could drift from the first.

**This is the strongest moment of the demo.**

exec: console.log('now open the Detail request and read the attempts table');

`expected_status` is the client's own success contract. Declaring 201 means a 200 counts as a failed delivery — the previous version resolved this field and then ignored it, accepting any 2xx.

request.description:
The core feature of this platform is that a client tells it which URL to call. That is a request-forgery primitive offered as a product.

Pointed here, the platform would fetch cloud credentials on the caller's behalf from inside the VPC and store the response in `notification_attempts.response_body` — where the caller can read it back through the self-service API.

Also try `https://127.0.0.1/hook`, `https://10.0.0.1/hook`, `http://client.example.com/hook`, and `https://user:pw@client.example.com/hook`.

**Note:** the local demo relaxes address-range blocking (`WEBHOOK_ALLOW_PRIVATE_NETWORKS=true`), because the demo webhook runs on a private Docker network. Set it to `false` in `.env` and restart the subscription service to see the full guard — both services log a warning at startup whenever it is relaxed.

item.name: 4 · Access control
item.description: Set the `client_id` variable to `CLIENT002`, run these, and watch resources that were readable a moment ago answer 404. The pre-request script re-fetches the token automatically.

request.description:
A token claiming `alg: none`, with a valid-looking `sub`, `aud` and `iss` and no signature at all.

Refused because the verification algorithm is pinned to HS256 in code rather than read from the token's own header. Without that pin, an attacker-controlled header decides how the token is verified — which is the `alg: none` forgery, and its cousin, RS256 downgraded to HS256.

Capture `notification_event_id` as CLIENT001, then switch the `client_id` variable to CLIENT002 and run this.

**404, not 403.** A 403 would confirm the id exists, turning the endpoint into an enumeration oracle.

In the previous version this returned the other client's payment payloads: the identity came from a query parameter, and the detail endpoint never compared the owner at all.

exec: pm.test('200 for the owner, 404 for anyone else', () =>
? 'refused — and indistinguishable from a nonexistent id'
: 'readable, because this is the owning client');

request.description: Ownership is part of the database lookup rather than a check applied to the result, so it cannot be forgotten at a call site — read and replay enforce it identically.

item.name: Load the fixture as settled history instead

request.description:
An alternative starting point to `deliver-all`: writes the ten fixture events with their recorded outcome — seven `DELIVERED`, three `FAILED` — so the list filters and the replay endpoint are populated instantly.

Running this first makes `deliver-all` a no-op, and correctly so: those events are already in terminal states and the dispatcher refuses to deliver an event twice. Use `make reset-events` to switch between the two.
